final_answer: No authority could be fetched and verified (every primary-source host was blocked by the network proxy), so under the citation firewall no authority is cited. The following is a provisional answer from background knowledge and is not firewall-verified. Short answer: probably yes as to the stated facts, but it turns on facts not given. Dispersing and arresting people at a peaceful, mostly sidewalk protest solely because of generalized fears of traffic disruption or 'potential escalation' is vulnerable under the First Amendment. Streets, sidewalks and plazas are traditional public forums. Government may impose content-neutral, narrowly tailored time/place/manner limits, and may disperse an assembly that is actually violent or presents an imminent threat of violence or serious obstruction. Edwards v. South Carolina, 372 U.S. 229 (1963), reversed breach-of-peace convictions of peaceful demonstrators who stayed after a police dispersal order, and Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444 (1969), limits punishing advocacy absent incitement to imminent lawless action. Verbal arguments, chanting, and occasionally stepping into the street are unlikely, standing alone, to supply the required imminence. Key open facts: whether the protest blocked traffic in a sustained way or posed a real safety hazard; whether a permit was required and obtained; which statute or ordinance was charged (for example Illinois mob action or disorderly conduct provisions, or a Chicago ordinance); whether the order identified a lawful basis and gave a reasonable opportunity and route to comply; and whether the dispersal order was content-neutral. If the protesters did obstruct traffic, the arrests for failure to disperse could be lawful as a time/place/manner enforcement. Remedies would likely be a Section 1983 claim and suppression or dismissal in the criminal case; qualified immunity and probable-cause (Fourth Amendment) arguments are separate considerations. I did not verify Illinois law or any Seventh Circuit authority.
